problem: The pipeline example is factually wrong for a standard pipeline. In a classic 5-stage pipeline, when instruction 1 is writing its result (WB), the instruction in the decode (ID) stage is three stages behind it, not instruction 2. As written, a student pictures two adjacent instructions in WB and ID at the same instant, which no pipeline does.
fix: Instruction level: a pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions, so while instruction 1 writes its result, a later instruction (three stages behind in a classic 5-stage pipeline) is decoding, and several instructions are in flight at once.

problem: 'Halving V cuts P four times' is ambiguous English; a student may read it as cutting power by 4 W or as four separate cuts.
fix: Halving V cuts P to one quarter (divides it by 4) at the same f.

problem: Carry look-ahead is a fair example of bit-level parallelism, but a carry-save adder is a way of deferring carries (used in multipliers), not an example of a wider word doing more work per operation. Listing it here blurs the definition.
fix: Bit level: a 64-bit adder works on 64 bit pairs in one operation instead of an 8-bit adder taking eight steps. Carry look-ahead adders are the classic example, since they compute all carries in parallel rather than letting one carry ripple through.
